Jensen is not just some male CEO. He’s an extraordinarily rare human being who spent 30 years making decisions that nobody else would’ve made, in circumstances that will never exist again, with a combination of abilities that cannot simply be reproduced

We’re talking about tech that could fundamentally alter the trajectory of human civilization. The implications extend so far beyond Nvidia’s market cap that we probably won’t fully comprehend them for generations

You could replace him tomorrow, but you could not recreate him in a thousand years

Not every disparity in human outcomes is a gender studies problem. Sometimes you’re just looking at a statistical freak of nature whose contributions to humanity are so consequential that reducing him to a demographic category isn’t just comically reductive, but is a sign that you profoundly misunderstand the scale of what you’re looking at

Early on in my career, this was my trick in interviews. 

I would meticulously research the person I was meeting with, find whatever I could about their personal interests online or through my network. 

I would try to naturally bring it up at the beginning of the interview and it immediately put them at ease, they felt connected to me, saw me as someone relatable and started off the meeting by them being net positive on me. 

Do this in customer meetings, investor meetings and everywhere else. Taking the time to understand people is worth it, everything going forward will be differentiated by emotional connection in a world of robotic interactions. 💭

candidates.text:
Soap operas started as a way to sell soap. I think microdramas could become the next big way to build a brand.

At ALZA last month, a friend who runs an agency in Europe gave me a rough number: around $250K to make an hour of high-quality microdrama. That’s a whole series a brand can release over time.

What interests me is the shift in what the brand is buying. A traditional ad has a short window to deliver a message. A series can give people a reason to spend time with the brand voluntarily.

I felt this with @echosabove, a young sneaker brand from Chennai. They made a short love story that begins when a woman notices someone’s shoes in a lift. The founder called it a massive risk, and it reached 9.9M views. I followed after watching it. 

I remember the cloud logo of the shoe. What stayed with me was the feeling of the film, the characters, and the brand behind it. I followed them because I wanted to see what they’d make next. They earned my attention before they ever asked me to buy a shoe. That, to me, is the win.

@Crocs  did something clever with Charmed to Meet You: Jibbitz charms are how two characters connect. The product has an actual role in the plot. Crocs reported nearly 8M views on @ReelShort_TV and went on to make a second season.

@marcjacobs did a great job with microdramas too. Its series The Scene introduced the Scene Bag through a scripted story rather than a conventional product campaign. 

But microdramas are getting crowded fast, and AI makes it easier for anyone to make one. Being able to produce a series won’t set a brand apart. The story will. People may forget the format, but they remember the characters, and the brand that was part of their story.

Music videos turned songs into worlds. 

I think microdramas could do that for brands, but only for the ones that make people want to come back for episode two.
